title: A subtype-specific gene regulatory program controls differential circuit integration of deep CA3 pyramidal neurons
authors: Daaboul, D.; Vandensteen, J.; Dascenco, D.; Lorente-Echeverria, B.; Vandenbempt, J.; Leysen, E.; Reverendo, M.; Vlaeminck, I.; Vervloessem, L.; Alcaraz, N.; Wojno, M.; Poovathingal, S.; Davie, K.; Magalhaes, P.; Kempynck, N.; Michel, G.; Spruston, N.; Wierda, K.; Aerts, S.; de Wit, J.
abstract: How closely related neuronal subtypes integrate into different circuits remains poorly understood. Deep and superficial hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons (PNs) differ in intrinsic firing and mossy fiber (MF) input at specialized postsynaptic structures termed thorny excrescences (TEs). Combining developmental single-nucleus multiomics with genetic targeting, morphological analysis and electrophysiology, we identify the transcription factor ST18 as a regulator of deep CA3 subtype identity. ST18 marks sparsely thorny and burst-firing neurons, and gene regulatory analyses predict that it represses a superficial-associated program involved in dendritic spine development, synaptic organization, and electrophysiological properties. Postnatal ST18 loss shifts the transcriptional and chromatin landscape of deep CA3 PNs toward a superficial-like state. These molecular changes are accompanied by increased TE elaboration approaching superficial levels, enhanced excitatory synaptic activity, and reduced burst-firing. Together, these findings identify ST18-dependent restriction of an alternative subtype program as a mechanism linking molecular identity to distinct input connectivity patterns and intrinsic firing properties during postnatal circuit maturation.

title: Learning to play with spikes: characterizing, predicting, and engineering unsupervised plasticity rules for spiking reservoir computing
authors: Kania, M.; Confavreux, B.; Vogels, T. P.
abstract: Spiking reservoir computing, and reservoir computing more generally, is a powerful and efficient framework for neuromorphic and biological applications, in which a fixed random reservoir drives a trained readout. Its performance depends critically on the reservoir initialization, so that enriching the reservoir with adaptive, unsupervised plasticity rules offers a natural solution to this limitation. However, it is unclear which rules work, or why, and how to find the best-suited rules for specific tasks without exhaustive and expensive search. Here, we learn how to play the Atari game Pong in a plastic spiking reservoir network. We systematically characterize a large family of local plasticity rules that were meta-learned in prior work. We then show that their performance is predictable and structured: high-scoring rules are characterized by strong differentiation between neurons encoding the ball trajectory and the background, with stable weight dynamics, and consistent readout alignment across time. These mechanistic signatures are not task-specific and transfer to a delayed-match recognition task. Rule performance can be estimated from rule parameters alone. Finally, conditioning simulation-based inference (SBI) on high scores allows us to sample directly from promising regions of the rule space, to discover rules that exceed the performance of those found in the prior distribution and reveal stable, high-performing configurations. Together, these results offer competitive performance against classical reservoir computing while providing a transparent, interpretable account of what makes a plasticity rule useful for neuromorphic hardware and biological computing.

title: FMRP safeguards long mRNA expression by opposing repressive RNP states
authors: Ma, K.; Hossain, A. R.; Judson, K. L.; Cheng, T. Q.; Greenblatt, E. J.
abstract: Fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) is widely viewed as a translational repressor, yet its loss paradoxically compromises expression of exceptionally long, dosage-sensitive neurodevelopmental mRNAs. First shown in Drosophila oocytes, this selective loss extends to mouse cortex and hippocampus, but its mechanism remains unknown. Here, we uncover a protective function for FMRP: shielding long mRNAs from repression by Me31B/DDX6, a conserved RNA helicase that organizes repressive RNP complexes. In Drosophila oocytes, FMRP loss redirects target mRNAs into Me31B-marked P-bodies. Transcriptome-wide binding maps reveal extensive FMRP-Me31B co-occupancy, preferentially concentrated on long coding sequences whose translation depends on FMRP. Strikingly, disrupting Me31B-dependent repression preferentially enhances translation of FMRP targets in FMRP-deficient oocytes. We identify Rin/G3BP, Caprin, and Lig/UBAP2L as FMRP-associated cofactors supporting expression of distinct targets. Together, our findings challenge the prevailing view of FMRP as a translational repressor, revealing instead a mechanism that safeguards vulnerable neurodevelopmental mRNAs from inappropriate cytoplasmic silencing.

title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
authors: Pourmirzaei, M.; Alqarghuli, S.; Chen, K.; Pourmirzaei, M.; Xu, D.
abstract: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

title: CryoSHIELDs: tunable amphipathic peptide additives for cryo-EM
authors: Azumaya, C. M.; Dutka, P.; Johnson, M. C.; Ravala, S. K.; Wu, C.-G.; Delgado, B. D.; Anson, F.; Michaelian, N.; Koo, C. W.; Tom, J. Y. K.; Soong, T. H.; Burt, A.; Ti, S.; Howes, A. C.; Martinez, O. E.; Song, A.; Rohou, A.; Ciferri, C.; Yatskevich, S.
abstract: While cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has transformed structural biology, sample preparation remains a major determinant of success. Specifically, the air-water interface (AWI) can damage complexes, impose preferred orientation, and reduce particle density. Here, we introduce cryoSHIELDs, a library of peptide additives designed to modulate the AWI and improve cryo-EM grid preparation. Across 24 diverse protein systems, cryoSHIELDs improved particle distribution, angular sampling, complex integrity, and, in selected cases, map quality and resolution. CryoSHIELDs enabled structure determination of the OSMR{beta}-Vixarelimab complex, the multi-subunit CCAN kinetochore complex without chemical cross-linking, and membrane proteins including ABCC6 and the -opioid receptor-Gi complex, the latter resolved at 2.3 A using tenfold lower protein concentration without compromising map quality. CryoSHIELDs provide a simple, tunable, and broadly applicable platform for more reliable cryo-EM in discovery biology and structure-based drug development.

title: Uncovering the latent structure of interwoven population and temporal codes
authors: Friedenberger, Z.; Cao, Y.; Naud, R.
abstract: Population analysis methods have become standard for navigating the complexity of neural data. However, these methods often assume a rate code, neglecting information encoded in the precise timing of spikes. Critically, additional information encoded in bursts of action potentials may be missed. Here, we develop a probabilistic latent-variable framework that disentangles the factors associated with bursts and individual spikes. This enables burst codes to be investigated directly from the structure of the data, without requiring external covariates. We demonstrate that analyzing firing rates alone obscures the latent structure and factors underlying bursts. Applying our method to simulated and experimental data, we show that it can infer the correct latent structure and be used to test for the presence of burst coding. By merging the population and burst coding perspectives, we provide a framework for linking changes in bursting to internal variables involved in attention, perception, and learning.

title: SF3b inhibitors suppress proliferation of nonsmall cell lung cancer cells irrespective of EGFR mutation status
authors: Fukagawa, W.; Horita, Y.; Harada, H.; Mori, M.; Murata, Y.; Ohe, K.
abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) are standard care for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but acquired resistance limits their durability, and alternatives that do not depend on EGFR kinase activity are needed. We asked whether inhibitors of SF3b, a core component of the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle, act on NSCLC cells regardless of EGFR genotype. Three lung adenocarcinoma lines were treated with pladienolide B or herboxidiene at 0.01, 0.1 and 1 uM: PC9 and HCC827, both carrying an EGFR exon 19 deletion and both inhibited by gefitinib at nanomolar concentrations, and A549, which is EGFR wild type and gefitinibin sensitive. Proliferation was followed for three days by crystal violet staining, EGFR intron 2 retention was assayed by RTPCR, and EGFR protein was measured by western blotting. Both compounds produced a concentration-dependent increase in the intron 2 retained product in all three lines, and both held proliferation at or near the day 0 cell number in all three, at concentrations down to 0.01 uM. EGFR protein was lost in PC9, reduced in A549, and only partly reduced in HCC827, where a residual band persisted in lanes whose growth was fully suppressed. Since A549 is EGFR wild-type, and published knockdown data show that removing EGFR does not suppress proliferation of wild-type lines, the growth inhibition cannot be attributed to loss of EGFR alone. We read EGFR intron 2 retention as a marker of target engagement rather than as the mechanism of the growth effect. These are the results of single experiments without replicates or statistical testing and should be read as preliminary.

title: LplA-mediated rescue of lethal myopathy and cardiomyopathy in mitochondrial lipoylation-deficient mammalian caused by Lipt1
authors: Yu, J.; Hu, Z.; Liu, Z.; Yang, R.; Zeng, A.
abstract: Inherited mitochondrial metabolic disorders impair cellular energy generation and often lead to fatal metabolic crises. Mitochondrial lipoylation defects represent a severe case of such disorders that can lead to lethality but lacks effective treatment so far. In this study, we generated a viable mouse model with muscle-specific deficiency of the lipoyltransferase coded by Lipt1 to provide an in vivo preclinical model that overcomes embryonic lethality. Using this model, we examined a bacterial lipoate protein ligase A (LplA)-mediated gene therapy via adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery. By introducing LplA alongside lipoic acid supplementation, we reconstituted a salvage pathway that bypasses the mammalian endogenous lipoylation pathway. The intervention rescued premature lethality, recovered motor function and reversed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the Lipt1-deficient mouse model. Mechanistically, AAV-LplA reconstitutes mitochondrial protein lipoylation and oxidative phosphorylation in situ. This energetic rescue suppresses phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-Akt hyperactivation, thereby restoring autophagic clearance and subsequently contributing to the recovery of the pathological phenotype. This study established AAV-LplA as a promising gene-delivery strategy for rescuing lethal mitochondrial lipoylation disorders.

title: Glycolytic enzymes form membrane-less condensates in the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum by sensing glucose levels
authors: Ishii, R.; Sakura, T.; Inaoka, D. K.; Tokumasu, F.
abstract: Recent studies have shown that liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in cells can regulate essential cellular events, including metabolic processes. Glycolytic bodies (G-bodies) are biomolecular condensates formed through the LLPS of glycolytic enzymes, and they accelerate glycolysis to overcome hypoxic stress in several organisms. Although the asexual blood stage (ABS) of the human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum highly depends on glycolysis for energy production, there have been no reports of the formation of such G-bodies throughout the parasite's lifecycle. Using fluorescence tagging and live imaging, we found that G-body-like condensates containing phosphofructokinase 9 (PFK9) and phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) were formed in the parasite cells after long-term culture under conditions of low glucose. These G-body-like structures appeared stable, but membrane staining and osmotic stress experiments suggested that the observed condensates were not associated with a lipid membrane. Notably, PFK9 and PGK formed spatially distinct, non-overlapping condensates, indicating that these structures were formed with different mechanism as compared to the shared, multi-enzyme G-bodies described in other organisms. Whether the condensation of these enzymes enhances or restrains glycolysis under low-glucose stress remains to be determined. These results suggest that the formation of glycolytic enzyme condensates may be an enzyme-specific cellular response that helps the parasite adapt to reductions in blood glucose levels in the host during the ABS.

title: High-throughput identification of chromatin-opening transcription factors
authors: Keith, A.; Jain, S.; Daza, R. M.; Qiu, C.; Germain, P.-L.; Shendure, J.; Domcke, S.
abstract: Cell fate transitions involve major changes to the chromatin landscape, some of which are thought to deepen the basin around a newly adopted cell state, stabilizing gene expression programs that might otherwise be transient. Transcription factors (TFs) are central to this process, binding only a subset of the genome-wide occurrences of their cognate motifs to create accessible regions that can act as cell type-specific enhancers. However, apart from a few well-studied cases, it is not clear which of the ~1,600 mammalian TFs can directly or indirectly initiate newly accessible sites, nor why only some motif occurrences gain accessibility. Here, we performed pooled CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) screens to upregulate endogenous developmental TFs in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) and assess their impact on the chromatin landscape. Following a pre-screen of 240 developmental TFs for their capacity to elicit strong changes to the transcriptome, we prioritized 60 TFs for a well-powered CRISPRa multiome screen in which we jointly profiled gene expression and chromatin accessibility across ~140,000 single cells. We identify TFs that appear to initiate new chromatin accessibility on their own ("autonomous"), others whose chromatin-opening activity appears dependent on coincident binding of co-TFs heterogeneously expressed across mESCs ("opportunistic"), and yet others which appear to induce a co-TF and then act alongside it ("hierarchical"). Taken together, our findings suggest that the ability of a TF to "pioneer" chromatin opening, when it is newly expressed at physiological levels, strongly depends on the cell state and gene regulatory network it lands in. Looking forward, a comprehensive charting of such dependencies will inform how cell fate transitions are initiated in development, homeostasis and disease, and how to engineer them in silico, in vitro and in vivo.

title: Molecular Characterization of T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia by an Optimal-Transport Based Multi-Omics Integration Framework
authors: Li, L.; Wang, J.; Wan, S.
abstract: T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy characterized by complex heterogeneity across multiple molecular layers. Accurate subtyping is essential for understanding disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and guiding targeted therapeutic strategies. However, current diagnostic approaches are labor-intensive and time-consuming, and existing computational methods are limited by reliance on single-modality data or simple integration strategies. Effective integration of heterogeneous multi-omics data remains a major computational challenge. We present OTTER (Optimal Transport-based Transcriptomics and gEnomics Representation), a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that jointly models transcriptomic and genomic data for T-ALL molecular characterization. OTTER encodes each omics modality through a modality-specific encoder and aligns the resulting latent representations using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT), which preserves the internal geometric structure of each modality without requiring a shared feature space. Benchmarking tests on the Children's Oncology Group (COG) AALL0434 cohort with >1,300 patients across 17 T-ALL subtypes suggested that OTTER significantly outperformed state-of-the-art approaches for T-ALL molecular characterization. In addition, OTTER could identify interpretable subtype-defining and omics-specific features for T-ALL. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the generalizability of OTTER by evaluating on multiple external independent clinical cohorts. In summary, OTTER provides a principled, biologically interpretable, and computationally effective framework for multi-omics driven T-ALL molecular characterization and broader cancer applications.

title: Dual kinase inhibition provides early clues to restoration of neuroimmune homeostasis in an AAV-haSyn model of Parkinsons disease
authors: Chiang, W.; Sandoval, I. M.; Li, H.; Bernal-Conde, L. D.; Squire, R.; Washburn, M. K.; Schwartz, J. L.; Squire, E.; Wagner, E. J.; Manfredsson, F. P.; Gelbard, H. A.
abstract: Background Previous studies of drugs targeting mixed linage kinase type 3 (MLK3) and/or leucine rich repeat kinase type 2 (LRRK2) in sporadic Parkinsons disease (PD) have failed to meet clinical endpoints despite multiple lines of evidence implicating these kinases in pathogenesis. This has reduced enthusiasm for MLK3 and LRRK2 as druggable targets. Largely overlooked is the evidence that these targets remain valid but must be considered in combination to achieve a therapeutic outcome. This provides the rationale for this study. Methods We conducted a pilot study modeling early, pre-symptomatic PD with subsequent evaluation of therapeutic potential of a multi-kinase inhibitor (URMC-099) in alleviating disease pathology. Sprague Dawley rats received unilateral intranigral injections of low dose AAV-haSyn. After a two-week recovery period, all animals were administered either once-daily intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of URMC-099 or its vehicle control until their terminal endpoint. Induction of early PD, and its alleviation with URMC-099, was evaluated by lateralized motor impairment using the cylinder test and immunohistochemical analysis of neuropathology in the substantia nigra (SN) and striatum. Finally, an in vitro microglial PD model exposed to aSyn pre-formed fibrils and treated with URMC-099 was used to further evaluate the mechanism underlying therapeutic activity. Results A unilateral model of early and progressive AAV-haSyn model for PD was used to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of a targeted multi-kinase inhibitor to attenuate PD-associated neuropathology and prevent the manifestation of lateral motor deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed protection of neuronal cellular integrity along the nigral-striatal pathway with once-daily i.p. URMC-099. The mitigation of degenerative neuropathology was linked to targeted inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2 and complemented by reduced levels of gliosis in astrocytes and microglia in the SN. Single-microglia segmentation analysis suggested URMC-099 treatment preserved dynamic effector state switching in microglia to enhance autophagic flux to reduce the overall burden of pathologic aSyn. Transcriptomic analysis of a complementary in vitro microglia model corroborated the retention of a homeostatic-like effector state with URMC-099 treatment that was unique to MLK3/LRRK2 dual inhibition. Conclusions Unilateral injection of low dose AAV-haSyn successfully resulted in a lateralized model of early, progressive PD. Dual inhibition of aberrant MLK3 and LRRK2 activity with once-daily i.p. URMC-099 therapy significantly mitigated the development of PD pathology and progression in an early manifest phenotype. Our results present a potential mechanism of therapeutic action dependent on the dual inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2. This presents a novel therapeutic modality that may be beneficial to a broad population of etiologic PD patients.

title: Shikonin alleviates bone cancer pain through suppression of spinal IGF2-associated p38 MAPK signaling

title: Feasible closed-loop stimulation for neural latent dynamics control
authors: Johnsen, K. A.; Lai, Y.; Vivekanandasarma, L.; Berman, G. J.; Pandarinath, C.; Rozell, C. J.
abstract: Modern neuroscience benefits from powerful computational and experimental methods for studying neural populations, including latent dynamics models that predict behavior with few dimensions. But despite their explanatory utility, latent factors are seldom targeted explicitly with experimental perturbations, leaving causal relationships to behavior and inferred dynamical landscapes untested. A promising solution is closed-loop, multi-channel optogenetic control, which, when paired with model predictions, could steer neural trajectories in real time--a feat impossible for traditional, hand-designed stimulation. However, because closed-loop latent control has not been demonstrated in vivo, the hardware and software requirements remain unclear--particularly the necessary stimulation dimensionality and how limited resources such as implant volume and bandwidth should be allocated between stimulation and recording capabilities. Preliminary experiments would thus help guide ongoing technological development. As large-scale exploration of these design spaces in vivo is prohibitively expensive, we conducted a high-throughput simulation survey using biophysically grounded spiking neural networks. We found that low-dimensional actuation is sufficient: in the reference configuration, ~20% of the stimulation channels achieved ~85% of peak control performance, far fewer than the number of neurons. Furthermore, allocating channels roughly equally between stimulation and recording optimized behavioral control, whereas pairing many electrodes with a single light source--the prevailing practice in experimental labs--performed poorly. Even without heavily optimizing modeling or control, we obtained >60% tracking error reduction and >90% evoked behavior accuracy on average for optimal channel counts. These results held across extensive parameter variations, suggesting that closed-loop latent control is feasible with accessible channel counts and establishing design principles for future tool development and in vivo experiments.

title: Identification of Kinome Biomarkers and Therapeutic Rescue in cGMP-Linked Retinal Degeneration
authors: Topcu Okan, I. C.; Ahmadian, M.; Altay, H. Y.; Pal Singh, S.; Kheirandish, G.; Ozer, S.; Gaillard, P.; Bouffard, R.; Neutzner, A.; Esmen, K.; Tschopp, M.; Lawrence, M.; Diril, M. K.; Paquet-Durand, F.; Agca, C.
abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations, such as Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) and Leber's congenital amaurosis (LCA), are major causes of progressive and irreversible vision loss. The large number of genes associated with these disorders makes their clinical and molecular characterization difficult, while systemic biomarkers for disease progression or treatment response remain limited. These challenges were addressed by targeting cGMP-associated mechanisms shared by RP and LCA and integrating systemic biomarker profiling with retinal outcomes. Kinase activity analysis (kinome analysis) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells distinguished healthy and diseased states and captured therapy-associated signatures in rd10 mice treated with LP-CN03, a liposomal formulation of the cGMP analog CN03. This first systemic analysis in a therapeutically responsive animal model highlights kinome analysis as a potential translational readout. Given shared cGMP signaling in RP and AIPL1-associated LCA, LP-CN03's therapeutic potential was further evaluated in a new CRISPR-Cas9-generated Aipl1-/- mouse model. Treatment with LP-CN03 preserved retinal structure and function, as shown by electroretinography, longitudinal optical coherence tomography, fundus imaging, optomotor testing, and photoreceptor-specific gene expression. Together, these findings provide independent in vivo evidence for the neuroprotective effect of LP-CN03 in both cGMP-related RP and LCA, also highlighting the translational value of kinome profiling.

title: Epidermal Langerhans Cells Act as Neuroimmune Regulators of Pain and Itch
authors: Sakai, K.; Ishida, H.; Pavlenko, D.; Suehiro, M.; Oshea, T.; Dorning, J.; Sanders, K.; Sanchez, C.; Lopez, A.; Talamas, S.; Boulina, M.; Griswold, A. J.; Akiyama, T.
abstract: Neuroimmune interactions in the skin coordinate immune defense and somatosensory perception, yet how immune cells shape sensory signaling remains poorly defined. Here, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), epidermal antigen-presenting cells, function as local immune-derived amplifiers of cutaneous sensory signaling. Anatomical and transcriptomic analyses reveal preferential LC association with non-peptidergic sensory neurons. LC activation increases neuronal and behavioral responses to thermal, mechanical, and pruritic stimuli without directly exciting sensory neurons, whereas LC inhibition or ablation selectively reduces pruritogen-evoked itch. We identified semaphorin 7A as a candidate LC-expressed mediator. Semaphorin 7A sensitized cultured sensory neurons to chloroquine and histamine, and neutralizing semaphorin 7A abolished the increase in chloroquine-evoked scratching produced by LC activation. Its receptor PlexinC1 was expressed by most MrgprA3 pruriceptors and blocking PlexinC1 reduced semaphorin 7A-evoked neuronal responses. Together, these findings identify epidermal LCs as local immune-derived amplifiers that regulate the responsiveness of cutaneous sensory circuits and identify semaphorin 7A as a mediator of LC-induced itch potentiation.

title: Sequential pathways preserve kinetochore integrity in meiosis
authors: Hamaia, M. C.; Spanos, C.; Borek, W. E.; Marston, A. L.
abstract: Kinetochores connect chromosomes to spindle microtubules, but how their integrity is maintained as they are remodelled during meiosis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify three distinct pathways linking centromeric chromatin to the outer kinetochore in budding yeast, mediated by the Ctf19 complex (Ctf19cCCAN), Mif2CENP-C and binding of Okp1CENP-Q-Ame1CENP-U to the Cse4CENP-A essential N-terminal domain (END). Although partially redundant during mitosis, all three connections are required during meiosis, with distinct temporal requirements. The assembled Ctf19cCCAN and Mif2CENP-C-dependent pathways maintain kinetochore integrity from meiotic entry, while Cse4CENP-A-Okp1CENP-Q-Ame1CENP-U binding becomes critical during prophase and the meiotic divisions. We further show that Ipl1Aurora B maintains kinetochore integrity independently of Ctf19cCCAN and provide evidence for an outer kinetochore-associated Ipl1Aurora B pool. Strikingly, Cse4CENP-A phosphomimetic mutations that restore kinetochore integrity upon Ipl1Aurora B depletion instead exacerbate defects in cells lacking Ctf19cCCAN. Our findings suggest that phosphorylation of the Cse4CENP-A N-terminal domain (NTD) by Ipl1Aurora B may regulate the use of alternative centromere-kinetochore connections to adapt to the changing requirements of meiosis.

title: SPACE-Tag Enables High-Throughput Spatial Chromatin Profiling With CUT&Tag
authors: Yan, C.; He, R.; Fernandez, S.; Pleska, M.; Maniatis, S.; Raimondi, I.; Vickovic, S.
abstract: Spatial epigenomics maps chromatin states within intact tissues, yet current methods remain limited by accessibility and scale. We developed SPACE-Tag, a spatial CUT&Tag framework that converts epigenetic marks-associated DNA into polyadenylated RNA through T7 based linear amplification, enabling direct integration with standard spatial transcriptomic workflows. Applied to the mouse brain, SPACETag resolved activating and repressive chromatin landscapes, recovered region-specific gene regulatory programs across anatomical domains, and showed strong correlation with existing bulk and single cell reference data. We generated an integrated multimodal atlas of the aging mouse brain, profiling five histone modifications and the transcriptome in parallel across the adult lifespan to establish the largest spatial multimodal dataset to date. This analysis uncovered sharp regional divergence with aging in the brain: fiber tracts showed widespread transcriptional downregulation, often without nearby chromatin state transitions, whereas the isocortex showed coordinated chromatin transcriptome changes, including an H3K4me1 peak module that increased with age, was enriched at super-enhancers and linked to upregulation of neuronal plasticity regulators. These findings highlight the power of multimodal and high throughput spatial genomics in uncovering the divergent regulatory logic that governs tissue-specific vulnerability and resilience in the aging brain.
